name: Cities and infrastructure
snapshot: I see cities and assets that need renewal. I would look for concessions, networks and maintenance with collectible revenue. The United States and Europe have different needs and permitting processes; fund holdings provide concrete evidence of exposure. Contractual exclusivity can help, but traffic, debt and cost overruns can hurt returns even when the project is necessary.
change: I am interested in how transport, housing, water and urban services are financed and maintained. A city can need a project for years without that need immediately turning into cash for the contractor.
arguments: Maintenance and long-term contracts can support demand and visibility.
Debt, competitive tenders and construction risk can leave little margin for shareholders.
invalidation: If usage, tariffs or contracted payments failed to cover maintenance and the cost of capital, I would reassess the thesis. In construction, I would also check whether cost overruns can be passed on to the customer.
value: I would look at concessions with clear rights, sufficient duration and verifiable demand. Exclusivity has conditions and an expiry date; I would distinguish the asset owner from the builder who takes on construction risk.
evidence_text: I retain the source’s definitions of city and megacity. For an investment, I would examine payment capacity, contracts and maintenance of the specific asset.

name: Robotics
snapshot: I see robots performing specific tasks, beyond demonstrations. I would look for useful operating hours, repeatable installations and recurring service. The United States and Europe provide safety rules and commercial evidence; capital includes funds and issuer buybacks. I focus on whether maintenance, integration or legal liability consume the savings, and how little actual robotics a listed company may contain.
change: A robot needs to work in the customer’s environment: moving, handling, cleaning or assisting safely. I look at actual availability and cost per task after installation, breakdowns and support.
arguments: Repetitive tasks in well-defined environments can produce savings and an installed base that generates service revenue.
Open environments, safety and support can make it difficult to replicate a successful pilot at scale.
invalidation: If useful working hours and renewals did not cover the total cost, I would reassess the thesis for that niche. An impressive video does not give me those metrics.
value: I would examine patents, training, instruments, service and the cost of switching an installed platform. That advantage requires checking competition and litigation. I would also examine what percentage of the business actually comes from robots.
evidence_text: I distinguish professional service robots, industrial robots and robotics-segment sales. The service figures relate to IFR’s sample, not an estimate of the entire industry. Mixing these populations can inflate the story without adding a single useful working hour.

name: Blockchain
snapshot: I see blockchain as a complete infrastructure: networks, payments, contracts, tokenisation, custody and applications. I would distinguish who uses the network from who earns revenue. Funds, issuers and banks provide different evidence of capital. The United States and Europe have different frameworks; I focus on the risk that activity grows without the chosen token or company capturing sustainable value.
change: I am interested in when a shared ledger allows value transfers, programmable agreements or asset settlement with less friction. Bitcoin, Ethereum, private networks and stablecoins solve different problems. In each case, I would ask who needs that architecture and who pays its costs.
arguments: Programmable settlement and shared infrastructure can reduce friction in specific use cases.
A conventional database can solve other cases at lower cost. Using a network does not necessarily make its token appreciate.
invalidation: If activity depended on subsidies, the customer did not pay or the right over a tokenised asset proved unenforceable, I would reassess the thesis. I would analyse the protocol, company, token and vehicle separately.
value: I would examine distribution, liquidity, licences, custody and connections with real-world money and assets. On open networks, a competitor can copy part of the code; I would ask what cannot be copied easily and who keeps the revenue.
evidence_text: I see higher average USDC and lower reserve income at Circle: +8% and −7.5% in Q3 2026 versus Q3 2025. This illustrates how interest rates affect one business line. I would not interpret it as a decline in total revenue or profit, both of which increased. Within blockchain, this case covers stablecoins, not the whole technology.

name: Quantum computing
snapshot: I see experimental progress and capital entering quantum computing. I would look for reproducible milestones and customers willing to pay for a useful advantage. The United States and Europe finance and regulate parts of the chain; a roadmap remains a target. I focus on cash consumption, dilution and the possibility that classical computing solves the same problem first.
change: Quantum computing seeks to solve certain classes of problems using a different architecture. I am interested in when it outperforms a classical alternative on a useful task at a competitive total cost. More qubits alone do not answer that question.
arguments: Error correction and joint work with classical computing can open scientific and commercial applications.
Timelines can lengthen, and the company needs funding while useful applications emerge. Classical methods are also advancing.
invalidation: If milestones could not be reproduced or the total cost remained uncompetitive for the chosen problem, I would reassess the commercial thesis. If cash ran out first, I would examine financing and dilution before anything else.
value: I would examine intellectual property, control systems, cryogenics, integration and contracts. I would not yet treat a lasting commercial monopoly across all quantum computing as established. A laboratory advantage needs to become a customer advantage.
evidence_text: I would keep observed results, surveys and announced targets separate.

name: Precious metals
snapshot: I see monetary demand for gold that includes central-bank purchases. I would track tonnes bought and sold by country, separately from price effects. Silver and platinum-group metals have a different demand mix. Vehicles offer different exposures; I focus on the risk of assuming official purchases guarantee returns or that all metals follow the same cycle.
change: I am interested in gold’s role as a reserve asset and a way to diversify official assets, alongside private investment and jewellery. For silver, platinum and palladium, I would also examine industrial demand and substitution. I would group them in one category while preserving those differences.
arguments: Reserve purchases can support demand for several years and reflect decisions that do not depend on the usual consumer.
Central banks can also sell. The price may already anticipate some of the demand, and the metal itself does not generate cash flow.
invalidation: If official purchases slowed or reversed on a sustained basis, I would reassess that support for the gold thesis. For each industrial metal, I would examine demand, substitution and marginal cost separately.
value: I would distinguish physical metal, vehicles that hold it in custody, miners, and royalty or streaming businesses. Gold has no monopolist. In a company, I would look for quality reserves, costs or contracts that are difficult to replicate, and calculate how much of the metal’s price increase reaches cash flow.
evidence_text: I track physical reserve purchases, investment and industrial demand separately. In gold, estimated total official purchases and the reported portion are not two amounts that can be added together.

geography.text: The Treasury reports 261,498,927 fine troy ounces in both September 2025 and September 2026. I read this as unchanged reserves, not new purchases.
The Czech central bank publishes reserve accumulation and its target of 100 tonnes by 2028. I would distinguish the target from completed purchases.
SAFE reports 75.44 million ounces in June and 77.47 million in September 2026. The increase equals approximately 63.14 tonnes, by my calculation.

policy.text: OFAC maintains the prohibition on importing Russian-origin gold under Executive Order 14068, with defined exceptions and references to licences. If accepted origins or sanctions changed, I would examine counterparties, custody and delivery terms before attributing the change to global scarcity.

The CNB links its purchases to gold supply-chain due diligence under Regulation (EU) 2017/821. I would see traceability as a condition of market access. It can favour accredited operators, although that alone does not prove pricing power.

moat_reading: I would distinguish physical metal, vehicles that hold it in custody, miners, and royalty or streaming businesses. Gold has no monopolist. In a company, I would look for quality reserves, costs or contracts that are difficult to replicate, and calculate how much of the metal’s price increase reaches cash flow.

moats.barrier: Quality reserves, permits, infrastructure and costs
moats.proof_status: Economic hypothesis to test for each asset; not a monopoly

moats.barrier: Long-lasting contracts, asset selection and access to capital
moats.proof_status: Verified contractual model; advantage and valuation remain to be assessed for each issuer

moats.barrier: Accreditation, scale, reputation and a counterparty network
moats.proof_status: Plausible barriers; no verified universal market share

further_analysis: If I chose a miner or a streaming business, I would examine the full cost, reserve life, contracts, debt and price paid. For metal held in custody, I would examine holder rights, custody, expenses and the vehicle’s availability.

capital.intro: I compare physical reserve changes and show who accumulates, reduces and maintains holdings. The country table comes from WGC; China and the United States are also checked against direct official data.
capital.coverage_note: The unreported portion of official demand is not allocated to countries. I would keep tonnes, ounces and dollar valuations separate.

glossary.definition: I would read it as financing in exchange for rights to buy part of future production on agreed terms. I would examine the upfront payment, the price per delivery and the operator’s ability to deliver.

I would read these as a contractual right to receive a portion of revenue, profit or another defined base from a mining operation. I would examine what is paid, for how long and what depends on the operator.

glossary_note: I would distinguish two contracts: streaming gives rights to buy future production in exchange for financing; royalties give the right to receive a portion of an agreed base. In both cases, I would examine the terms and the operator’s delivery capacity.
